the distracted fallback operator does not intervene in time
the vehicle strikes and kills the pedestrian.

reach.local: A pedestrian is struck and killed by an automated test vehicle.

coverage.note: Multiple records inform particular components, not the complete pathway. Studies, announcements and historical non-AI comparisons are identified by setting; record counts do not measure evidence strength or independent replication.

pathways.title: Unguarded tutoring improves assisted performance but worsens subsequent unaided work
pathways.endpoint: reduced subsequent unaided mathematics performance in the studied setting.
pathways.basis: O plus R mediator, [ED], with [EC] affiliation correction; reduced subsequent unaided mathematics performance in the studied setting.
pathways.conditions: The experiment supports the intervention/outcome contrast in one Turkish high school; the learning-process mediator is R, not established simply by the performance result. It does not demonstrate durable population-wide deskilling.
pathways.barrierCandidates: The teacher-informed GPT Tutor package largely avoided the measured negative effect, without establishing an unaided-exam improvement over control. The package bundled design changes, so do not attribute efficacy to one isolated feature. Replication and longer-term learning outcomes would be required for wider claims.

steps.text: Students receive an unrestricted GPT-based practice tool
assisted practice performance improves
reliance on supplied answers may displace productive independent practice
after access is removed, unaided exam performance is worse than the control condition.

reach.local: Students perform worse on an unaided examination after unrestricted AI-assisted practice.

coverage.note: Multiple records inform particular components, not the complete pathway. Studies, announcements and historical non-AI comparisons are identified by setting; record counts do not measure evidence strength or independent replication.

typology.title: Causal-role typology
typology.basis: An Auspex adaptation of bow-tie risk analysis. Mechanisms, propagation and consequence distance extend its hazard–threat–loss-of-control–consequence structure. These are editorial annotations of the cited pathways, not classifications supplied or endorsed by their authors.

roles.label: Condition
roles.definition: A capability, dependency, incentive or setting that makes the pathway possible. Its presence alone does not establish harm.

roles.label: Trigger
roles.definition: An action, shock or change that initiates or reactivates an adverse sequence. It need not be accidental.

roles.label: Mechanism
roles.definition: How an action or state produces the next effect, such as optimization, deception or dependence.

roles.label: Control failure
roles.definition: A specified boundary, safeguard or corrective capacity becomes ineffective. Several distinct control failures can occur in one pathway.

roles.label: Propagation
roles.definition: A feedback loop, transfer or dependency carries an existing effect into other systems, actors or repeated decisions.

roles.label: Intermediate effect
roles.definition: A changed state or measured outcome that is not itself established as harmful, but matters to the subsequent argument.

roles.label: Proximal harm
roles.definition: A directly described injury, deprivation or loss of agency in the selected causal account. Proximal does not mean minor, local or soon.

roles.label: Distal harm
roles.definition: A further harmful consequence mediated by additional processes, feedback or loss of recovery. Distal does not mean global, inevitable or existential.

rules: Roles describe causal function, not a fixed ladder. They can recur, overlap or be absent. Arrows retain the source account’s conditional ordering.
Proximal/distal describes causal distance within this account. Geographic reach, elapsed time, severity and reversibility are separate properties.
An observed component does not validate its containing pathway. Evidence and uncertainty remain attached to the specific incident, component or connection.

Studies, deployed events and mechanism comparisons retain distinct settings. A study series counts once even when it examines several models or safeguards. Mappings across pathways are not independent incidents.

references.title: MIT AI Risk Repository · Entity, intent and timing
CSET · Adding Structure to AI Harm
Bucknall & Dori-Hacohen · Current and Near-Term AI as a Potential Existential Risk Factor
references.note: AIES 2022; conducted during Bucknall’s ERO research internship. A hypothesis about mediating risk factors, not validation of their catastrophic continuation.

references.title: Koopmanschap & Barten · How to Catch a GPU
references.note: ERO hardware-governance taxonomy. Technical feasibility of controlling AI accelerators; institutional adoption and response to detected violations are outside its analysis.

references.title: Chin · Dimensional Characterization and Pathway Modeling for Catastrophic AI Risks
references.note: Separates scenario pathways from seven dimensions. Its categories and illustrative paths are explicitly non-exhaustive.

barrierRoles.label: Prevention
barrierRoles.definition: Acts before the specific unwanted action or boundary crossing being assessed.

barrierRoles.label: Containment
barrierRoles.definition: Interrupts activity or limits further consequences after the assessed breach or onset.

barrierRoles.label: Detection & response
barrierRoles.definition: Identifies an event and brings an appropriate intervention into action.

barrierRoles.label: Execution limit
barrierRoles.definition: Ends a run or resource allocation. This does not by itself revoke access, remove copies or repair harm.

aiStages.label: AI development
aiStages.definition: Training, objective formation and successor development determine what behavior is selected and inherited.

aiStages.label: Evaluation & oversight
aiStages.definition: Tests, monitoring, procurement and review affect which systems or actions are accepted as safe.

aiStages.label: Deployment & delegation
aiStages.definition: People grant systems consequential roles, permissions or decision authority.

aiStages.label: Optimization & error
aiStages.definition: A model pursues a proxy, generates a systematic error or produces a harmful recommendation.

aiStages.label: Access & execution
aiStages.definition: AI assistance, privileged access or executable activity reaches a consequential system.

aiStages.label: Persistent operation
aiStages.definition: Execution, copies, resources or access survive attempts to interrupt activity.

aiStages.label: Resource & capability scaling
aiStages.definition: Compute, labor substitution, physical production or practical capability expands what an actor can do.

aiStages.label: Information & beliefs
aiStages.definition: AI-mediated advice, ranking or persuasion changes what people see, believe or can verify.

aiStages.label: Institutional dependence
aiStages.definition: Organizations or people lose independent alternatives, skills or bargaining power as AI-mediated functions become essential.

aiStages.label: Command & authority
aiStages.definition: A principal directs coercive action or acquires political authority, including through a human launch decision.

aiStages.label: Feedback & coordination
aiStages.definition: Interacting agents, institutions or shared dependencies amplify effects or obstruct collective action.

aiStages.label: Safety boundary
aiStages.definition: A relevant legal, technical, physical or organizational constraint is crossed or becomes ineffective.

aiStages.label: Harmful exposure
aiStages.definition: Digital decisions produce consequential exposure, service deprivation or physical damage.

aiStages.label: Response & recovery
aiStages.definition: Detection, intervention, substitutes and restoration determine whether the disruption can be reversed.

aiStages.label: Terminal consequence
aiStages.definition: The endpoint specified by this scenario; its severity and reversibility depend on its stated conditions.

typology.aiBasis: AI-specific mechanism stages are editorial crosswalks to the source scenarios. Development, access, resource scaling, institutional dependence and collective response distinguish where AI changes the causal story. These stages may repeat and branch; they are not a universal escalation ladder. Causal roles remain a separate facet.

enforcement.title: What changes as AI becomes more capable?
enforcement.scope: ERO’s taxonomy concerns international agreements controlling AI accelerators. Applying its dependency questions to incident barriers is an editorial comparison; the paper does not establish that a model refusal or account ban enforces such an agreement.

questions.label: Resource access
questions.text: Can the actor obtain equivalent capability through new accounts, other providers, local models or unmonitored hardware?

questions.label: Hidden capacity
questions.text: Would the defender detect the execution or physical capacity needed for the harmful action as its footprint shrinks?

questions.label: Escape from control
questions.text: Does intervention cover every consequential execution route, or only the activity still visible inside the controlled system?

enforcement.limit: The paper identifies falling compute requirements as a source of enforcement fragility. It does not assess legal adoption, mutual verification or the response needed after detecting a violation.
